lead: >-
  On the current itinerary combining Brazil and Paraguay, the cultural programme is concentrated chiefly in Paraguay: historic Asunción, the Museo del Barro, Indigenous communities and Mennonite settlements in the Chaco, Areguá's crafts and the history of the colonies of Guairá. ## How Paraguayan and Brazilian culture come together on one route

This selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. Its current basis is the [tour of Uruguay and Paraguay with a visit to Iguazú](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/). The page title highlights [Brazil](/brazil/) and [Paraguay](/paraguay/) as countries sharing a route and theme, but the actual journey begins in Uruguay and ends at the waterfalls on both the Brazilian and Argentine sides. It is not a separate sightseeing programme limited to two countries.

The cultural days are distributed unevenly. Paraguay offers museums, urban history, communities and craft-producing settlements. The Brazilian section features tropical forest, waterfall panoramas and the [Bird Park](/brazil/foz-do-iguacu/iguazu-bird-park-tour-6-hours/). The falls have their own natural significance, but the tour does not promise a separate cultural and historical exploration of Rio de Janeiro, Salvador or Brazil's colonial towns at this stage.

| Route section | Main cultural experience |
|---|---|
| Asunción | Independence history, museum and architecture |
| Chaco | Mennonite and Indigenous communities, memories of the war |
| Areguá and Guairá | Crafts, settlements and local history |
| Brazilian Iguazú | Natural heritage and forest, without a separate museum programme |

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_tur_po_uruguayu_i_paragvayu_16_dnej}}

## Asunción: from the Museo del Barro to the House of Independence

A flight from Montevideo brings travellers to [Asunción](/paraguay/place/asuncion/). On arrival day, the programme includes the Museo del Barro and a private introduction to the historic centre. The museum's collections bring together folk art, contemporary artistic culture and works by Paraguay's Indigenous peoples. Visitors can see how craft and artistic traditions continue within a modern city.

The following city tour includes López Palace, the National Pantheon of Heroes and the Independence House Museum. The latter is devoted to the events of 1811 and helps explain the formation of the Paraguayan state. It makes more sense to view these buildings as a connected history of the capital than merely as stops for photographs.

In the afternoon, lunch beside the water and a walk on the nature trails of Puerto Olivares are scheduled. Cultural and nature experiences thus alternate even in Asunción. For more geographical options, explore [Paraguay tours](/paraguay/tour/) and [the country's culture and history itineraries](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/paraguay/).

## Chaco: several cultures on one dry plain

After the capital, the route heads into [Paraguay's Chaco](/paraguay/place/chaco/). Travelling via [Filadelfia](/paraguay/place/filadelfia/), visitors see the [Fortín Toledo conservation centre](/paraguay/place/fortin-toledo-reserve/) and memorial sites associated with the Chaco War. The memorials recall the conflict between Paraguay and Bolivia in the 1930s. That stop belongs to the historical part of the journey, while the reserve introduces the nature surrounding the settlements.

The next day links [Laguna Capitán](/paraguay/place/laguna-capitan/) with Mennonite communities. The programme explains how settlers developed a region with scarce water, building roads, schools and cooperatives. Another day is set aside for a visit to an Indigenous community and the Filadelfia Museum. Comparing these experiences reveals different ways of living on the same land, without turning local people into a tourist performance.

It is useful to discuss in advance exactly what a community visit involves: permission to take photographs, the form of the presentation, whether an interpreter is needed and rules for respectful interaction. The general itinerary is known, but private meetings and demonstrations not mentioned in the programme should not automatically be counted as included.

## Areguá and Colonia Independencia: crafts and immigrant heritage

On the way out of Asunción, the programme visits [Areguá](/paraguay/place/aregua/), known for craft shops and ceramics. The journey then goes through San Bernardino to [Colonia Independencia](/paraguay/place/colonia-independencia/) in the Guairá region. Here, German settler traditions have become part of everyday local life. The tour introduces settlements, architecture and regional history; the following day includes lunch and a return to Asunción.

This section should not be confused with a visit to Paraguay's Jesuit missions. Those monuments do exist, but the selected itinerary does not include them. Instead, it focuses on present-day communities, crafts, museums and Chaco memorial sites.

## Brazil: why Iguazú completes a cultural journey

The journey via [Ciudad del Este](/paraguay/place/ciudad-del-este/) leads to [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). Here the subject changes: Paraguay's dry expanses give way to humid Atlantic Forest. The Brazilian side of Iguazú offers wide views of the cascades. The national park protects a large area of Atlantic Forest with diverse plants and wildlife.

The itinerary also includes a separate excursion to the [Bird Park](/brazil/foz-do-iguacu/iguazu-bird-park-tour-6-hours/); its terms and format are given on the excursion page. Travellers then visit the Argentine side of the falls and Devil's Throat. There are thus more border crossings than the name of this two-country selection might suggest.

This sequence makes sense: after Paraguay's independence history, settlements and museums, travellers spend a day at a natural landmark of continental importance. If Brazilian culture is your main priority, compare [cultural tours in Brazil](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/brazil/), which may have fundamentally different geography and itineraries.

## Planning travel and border crossings

The programme separately identifies a flight from Uruguay to Asunción, road journeys into the Chaco, a flight to Ciudad del Este and the overland crossing to Brazil. The next stage is an excursion to the Argentine side of Iguazú. These transfers take time that cannot all be allocated to museums and walks.

For this journey, Ada Tours coordinates the sequence of trips and transfers, while document requirements are checked against each traveller's nationality and actual ports of entry. Entry rules for Paraguay, Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina may differ; permission for one country does not by itself establish the right to visit the others. It is also useful to discuss local spending currencies and payment options along the route in advance, without assuming that any particular bank card will work.

For all itineraries including both countries, consult the [Brazil + Paraguay selection](/multi-country/brazil_paraguay/). Other combinations with cultural programmes appear under [multi-country culture and history tours](/multi-country/interests/culture-and-history/) and in the [general cultural travel section](/interests/culture-and-history/).

## Frequently asked questions about the culture of Brazil and Paraguay

### Is this a separate tour covering only Brazil and Paraguay?

No. The current [16-day programme](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/) begins in Uruguay, travels through Paraguay and the Brazilian side of Iguazú, and includes a visit to the Argentine side of the falls.

### Which Paraguayan cultural attractions are included?

The Museo del Barro, historic attractions in Asunción, Chaco War memorials, Mennonite settlements in the Chaco, an Indigenous community, Filadelfia, Areguá and the colonies of Guairá. The exact sequence is shown day by day in the [tour programme](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/).

### Are museums or historic Brazilian cities scheduled?

The Brazilian stage includes Iguazú and associated nature excursions. The itinerary does not contain a separate visit to Rio museums, historic Salvador or Brazil's Jesuit missions.

### Can we spend more time with communities in the Chaco?

Additional time and specific permitted meetings can be discussed when tailoring the route. Their availability, arrangements and terms must be agreed separately; they are not included by default in the programme described.

## What the food and wine theme means for Brazil + Paraguay

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} featuring both countries under the “Food and Wine” interest. The selection is based on a [16-day tour through Uruguay, Paraguay and Iguazú Falls](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/). It also includes the Argentine side of the falls. Choosing it as a separate two-country journey exclusively devoted to restaurants and wineries would therefore be misleading.

The full journey genuinely includes a substantial gastronomic experience. But it is primarily connected with the [wineries of Canelones in Uruguay](/uruguay/place/canelones/), where a tasting and lunch among the vineyards are scheduled. In Paraguay, the focus shifts to local settlements, their traditions and regional food. The Brazilian finale revolves around [Iguazú](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/), forest and nature excursions.

| Geography | What is included and what can be discussed |
|---|---|
| Uruguay, Canelones | Boutique winery visit, Tannat tasting, lunch |
| Paraguay, Asunción | Lunch at Puerto Olivares, cultural programme |
| Paraguay, Guairá | Visits to colonies; regional winemaking traditions are described, but no separate tasting is specified |
| Brazil, Foz do Iguaçu | Falls and excursions; no separate culinary workshop is specified |

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_tur_po_uruguayu_i_paragvayu_16_dnej}}

This arrangement is particularly interesting for those who see food as part of discovering a country. However, **the gastronomic theme belongs to the whole itinerary**; it does not guarantee a restaurant tour or wine tasting in each of the selected countries.

## Paraguayan cuisine: chipa, sopa paraguaya and home traditions

In [Paraguay](/paraguay/), local culinary traditions are closely linked to maize, cassava, cheese and Guaraní culture. Well-known dishes include *chipa*, a cheese bread made with cassava starch, and *sopa paraguaya*. Despite the word “soup”, the latter is baked maize dough with cheese and onion. Another characteristic dish is *mbejú*, a flatbread made with starch and cheese.

These dishes help explain Paraguayan cuisine, but the published programme **does not include a special chipa tasting, cooking class or guaranteed menu featuring these particular items**. They can be discussed when arranging meals, while keeping a distinction between the country's characteristic food and the services already paid for on the specific tour.

The Paraguayan stage begins in [Asunción](/paraguay/place/asuncion/). After the Museo del Barro and historic buildings, the itinerary includes lunch by the water at the Puerto Olivares ranch. This forms part of a day devoted to city history and nature trails, rather than a dedicated multi-stop food tour.

## Chaco: food and everyday life in Mennonite and Indigenous communities

Next, travellers head to the [Chaco](/paraguay/place/chaco/) via [Filadelfia](/paraguay/place/filadelfia/). Settlement history here is closely tied to the challenge of farming in a dry environment. Mennonite settlers developed farms, cooperatives, roads and schools. Community visits and a local museum offer an introduction to their experience.

A separate stage includes a meeting with an Indigenous community in the Chaco. The visit focuses on the lives and crafts of its members. It must not automatically be turned into an “Indigenous cuisine tasting”: if a particular dish, home-cooked meal or cooking activity is not mentioned in the itinerary, it must be agreed separately with the organisers and hosts.

Understanding the region's food history can be more meaningful than a routine restaurant stop. Local farming methods, access to water and traditions of cooperation matter. They provide context for the food travellers try while journeying through the country.

## Guairá: German colonies and small wineries

After [Areguá](/paraguay/place/aregua/) and San Bernardino, the route reaches [Colonia Independencia](/paraguay/place/colonia-independencia/) in the Guairá region. The area is associated with German immigrant traditions and local artisanal winemaking. The day's description explicitly mentions visitors coming to sample regional wines.

There is, however, an important distinction between a description of the region and the services included. Day 12 specifies visits to the colonies and lunch at Tylinsky. **A visit to a named winery, a tasting flight and transfer to a tasting are not separately confirmed for that day.** If Guairá wine is your main priority, consider adding it when the itinerary is agreed.

Guairá wines should not be confused with the Tannat of Canelones. The latter belongs to the Uruguayan stage of the same journey, and that is where a tasting is explicitly listed. The two regions differ both geographically and in the activities scheduled.

## Brazilian Iguazú: a nature-focused finale and dinner possibilities

After travelling from [Ciudad del Este](/paraguay/place/ciudad-del-este/), visitors arrive in [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). The main programme here involves national park panorama trails and the [Bird Park](/brazil/foz-do-iguacu/iguazu-bird-park-tour-6-hours/). The next day brings a visit to the Argentine side of the waterfalls.

Brazilian cuisine can also be explored on this part of the trip. Dishes based on beans, rice, cassava and meat are popular in the country, and flavours vary considerably by region. But the approved Brazilian itinerary **does not include a separate restaurant tour, caipirinha-making class or included tasting**. This could be an idea for a free evening, but must not be counted as a paid-for tour activity.

If Brazilian gastronomy is your main reason for travelling, compare the country's [food and wine tours](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/brazil/) and the wider [gastronomic travel section](/interests/food-and-wine/). Another route may devote a much larger proportion of its days to the theme.

## Choosing a route with food experiences

When comparing programmes, ask a simple question: do you want to discover several countries while trying local food along the way, or devote most days to tastings and working with chefs? The itinerary described here is primarily suited to the first approach.

Before confirming the journey, discuss dietary preferences, vegetarian meals or allergen restrictions, as well as the desired number of special restaurant evenings. Travel through Asunción, the Chaco, Guairá and Iguazú takes considerable time. More elaborate culinary additions need to fit around the scheduled transfers and excursions.

Other current options featuring both countries appear in the [Brazil and Paraguay selection](/multi-country/brazil_paraguay/), while [multi-country food and wine tours](/multi-country/interests/food-and-wine/) offer a wider geographical choice.

## Frequently asked questions about the food of Brazil and Paraguay

### Is a wine tasting included on the current tour?

Yes. A tasting at a boutique winery is included during the visit to Canelones in **Uruguay**. No wine tasting in Paraguay is separately specified, despite the introduction to Guairá's winemaking traditions.

### Is a tasting of Paraguay's national dishes included?

There is no separate food excursion or fixed tasting menu. Lunches are specified at certain stages of the journey, but the exact dishes are not listed.

### Is there a culinary class in Foz do Iguaçu?

The Brazilian section describes waterfalls and nature excursions. No cooking class or tasting is specified.

### Can gastronomy be the main theme of the journey?

Yes. Markets, restaurants and wineries can be discussed for a tailor-made programme, but that would change the route and services, rather than describe the published 16-day tour.

## Nature in Brazil and Paraguay: from the Chaco to Iguazú Falls

**Paraguay offers the Chaco's dry forests, saline lagoons and the hills of Guairá on this route. Brazil adds humid forest and Iguazú Falls.** These landscapes lie at different stages, so discovering them takes time and more than a single sightseeing excursion.

Our selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. The current option is a [16-day journey through Uruguay, Paraguay and Iguazú](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/). Travellers start with time in Uruguay, then fly to Asunción, explore areas of Paraguay and finish near the waterfalls on the border between Brazil and Argentina. This is **an intersection of two countries within a wider itinerary**, not a separate tour with a direct flight from Paraguay to the falls.

The [general Brazil + Paraguay catalogue](/multi-country/brazil_paraguay/) shows journeys regardless of interest. Here, the focus is on nature, confirmed stops and practical conditions.

## Paraguay: the dry Chaco, birds at Laguna Capitán and Guairá

Following the historical programme in Asunción, travellers head for the [Chaco](/paraguay/place/chaco/) on day eight. The route includes Filadelfia and [Fortín Toledo](/paraguay/place/fortin-toledo-reserve/). The region is characterised by dry forests, plains, hot air and long distances between settlements. The journey from the capital takes about four hours, so walks need to be scheduled around the drive.

The next day, the group visits [Laguna Capitán](/paraguay/place/laguna-capitan/), where waterbirds, including flamingos, may be observed. Encounters depend on water levels, weather and season; an excursion does not guarantee a particular species at a particular hour. Paraguay's national tourism authority presents the Chaco and Laguna Capitán as nature destinations that can be combined with historical stops.

After the Chaco, the route continues through Guairá's hilly terrain and the [Ybytyruzú mountain range](/paraguay/place/ybytyruzu-mountain-range/). This brings another change of landscape before the Brazilian border. For travellers interested in nature, this section adds much more to the programme than a short transfer between Asunción and Ciudad del Este would.

## Brazil: Iguazú after Paraguay's plains

On day thirteen, the route reaches Ciudad del Este and then [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) on the Brazilian side of the border. After the dry Chaco, conditions change to humid vegetation, a river valley and cascades surrounded by tropical forest.

Day fourteen includes sightseeing on **the Brazilian side of Iguazú**, walks along the paths, the Macuco Safari boat excursion and the Bird Park. Panoramic viewpoints on the Brazilian side reveal the wide expanse of cascades; the boat brings visitors closer to the flowing water, while the Bird Park focuses on tropical fauna. These activities differ in physical demands and safety requirements.

The following day includes **the Argentine side of Iguazú** and Devil's Throat. This involves another border crossing. Although the article focuses on Brazil and Paraguay, the complete programme cannot be described without Argentina.

| Area | Main attraction |
|---|---|
| [Chaco](/paraguay/place/chaco/) | Dry forests and plains |
| [Laguna Capitán](/paraguay/place/laguna-capitan/) | Birds and shallow water |
| [Guairá](/paraguay/place/ybytyruzu-mountain-range/) | Green hills |
| [Iguazú](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) | Humid forest and waterfalls |

## Sequence, weather and physical demands

In the Chaco, account for long drives, heat and sun exposure. Lightweight long-sleeved clothing, a hat and drinking water are useful. At Iguazú, waterproof protection for belongings, non-slip footwear and a raincoat are needed. Conditions on the boat excursion differ from those on ordinary raised walkways.

The volume of water at Iguazú depends on rainfall, so the falls look different at different times. Access to particular trails and boat services also depends on local restrictions. At Laguna Capitán, watching birds calls for time and quiet behaviour rather than a brief photo stop.

The programme combines several kinds of outdoor travel. Dry and humid regions, a lagoon and waterfalls should each be assessed by the actual duration of the day's activities. If birdwatching is your priority, focus on the Chaco; if waterscapes matter most, look at the final days around Iguazú.

## Arrangements and actual inclusions

The [full itinerary](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/) specifies flights, accommodation, transport, excursions and separate exclusions. Do not copy terms from other trips in the country: the time allowed at the lagoon, language of guides and precise content of boat outings belong to this particular journey.

Documents need to be checked **for every country actually visited**: Uruguay, Paraguay, Brazil and Argentina. Visa and border rules depend on nationality. A trip limited to two countries would require a separate itinerary and price.

For other nature-focused options, see [Paraguay nature tours](/interests/nature/tours/paraguay/) and [Brazil nature tours](/interests/nature/tours/brazil/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Does this itinerary cover only Brazil and Paraguay?

No. The [16-day tour](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/) begins in Uruguay, continues through Paraguay and Brazil, and includes a visit to the Argentine side of Iguazú.

### Where can birds be observed?

In Paraguay, chiefly at [Laguna Capitán](/paraguay/place/laguna-capitan/). The Brazilian stage includes the Bird Park. Watching birds in their natural habitat and visiting an organised park are different activities.

### When will travellers see Iguazú?

The Brazilian side is scheduled for day fourteen and the Argentine side for day fifteen. Conditions on the trails and water excursions should be checked closer to the trip.

## The Chaco and Iguazú on one tour: two natural worlds of South America

This selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} involving nature in Brazil and Paraguay. On the current [16-day Uruguay, Paraguay and Iguazú itinerary](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/), the “Nature and Wildlife” theme is especially evident in two areas: the dry landscapes of the [Chaco](/paraguay/place/chaco/) and the humid forests around [Iguazú Falls](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/).

The combination makes it possible to compare natural zones. Climate, vegetation and the appearance of water bodies change between the two. In the Chaco, conserving rare animals and protecting saline lagoons are important; around Iguazú, a powerful river, cascades and multi-level tropical forest dominate.

| Area | What the itinerary includes |
|---|---|
| Paraguayan Chaco | Tagua peccary conservation centre at Fortín Toledo Reserve |
| Laguna Capitán | A walk to a saline lake where flamingos and swans may occur |
| Guairá region | Forested mountain trails and waterfalls |
| Foz do Iguaçu, Brazil | Panoramic paths by the falls, nature excursions and the Bird Park |

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_tur_po_uruguayu_i_paragvayu_16_dnej}}

The journey begins in Uruguay and, after the Brazilian section, includes the Argentine side of Iguazú. Thus **the two countries in the selection title do not mean that the other stages of the full programme are absent**.

## Fortín Toledo: protecting the tagua in Paraguay's Chaco

After Asunción, the journey heads into the [Chaco](/paraguay/place/chaco/) via [Filadelfia](/paraguay/place/filadelfia/). On the way, travellers see scattered settlements and dry plains with shrubs and patches of forest. Life here is distinctive: plants and animals are adapted to heat, prolonged dry periods and scarce water.

The afternoon includes [Fortín Toledo Reserve](/paraguay/place/fortin-toledo-reserve/). Its conservation work focuses on the tagua, or Chacoan peccary, a rare animal native to this region. The tour description also mentions armadillos, foxes, anteaters and various birds found in the Chaco.

However, a list of species living in the region **is not a promise that visitors will see every one on an excursion**. Observation depends on the animals' behaviour, weather and the route through permitted areas. Fortín Toledo's principal value for travellers lies in learning about local conservation work and its relationship to the dry forest ecosystem.

The same day includes Chaco War memorials. The ecological and historical stops are close to each other, making this a broader experience than an ordinary reserve visit.

## Laguna Capitán: flamingos in saline shallows

The following morning, travellers head to [Laguna Capitán](/paraguay/place/laguna-capitan/), a very different natural site. Along pale saline shores and in shallow water, waterbirds and shorebirds can be seen; the programme specifically mentions flamingos and swans.

Flamingos remain wild animals. The number of birds, their distance from shore and the opportunity for a photograph vary. Approaching them closely or counting on a guaranteed shot is inappropriate. Binoculars, drinking water, a hat and sun protection are more useful.

Later, the day focuses on Mennonite settlements. Travellers learn how people developed the dry region and established farms despite water shortages. This creates a natural connection between the environment and the history of settlement in the Chaco.

## Guairá's forests and nature trails

Another Paraguayan section runs through Areguá and San Bernardino to [Colonia Independencia](/paraguay/place/colonia-independencia/) and the Ybytyruzú mountain area. The programme includes trails through forested slopes, waterfalls and viewpoints.

The main expectations for a Guairá walk are mountain landscapes and vegetation. The day's description does not include a specialised search for rare animals, a night safari or an ornithological tour with a confirmed species list.

Comfortable trail shoes and some allowance for weather changes are useful. The length and difficulty of the walks should be discussed with regard to travellers' fitness and the actual route for the day.

## Brazilian Iguazú: humid forest, cascades and birds

After flying to Ciudad del Este, travellers cross to the Brazilian side and stay in [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). The forest around the falls belongs to Brazil's Atlantic Forest region. Instead of the dusty roads of the Chaco, there is dense greenery, humid air and the sound of falling water.

The following day includes a panoramic tour along the falls. The main purpose of the walk is to see the long chain of cascades, islands between the flows and great clouds of spray rising over the gorge. Clothing can become wet at viewpoints, and paths may be slippery.

The programme includes a separate excursion to the [“Exotic Bird Park in Iguazú”](/brazil/foz-do-iguacu/iguazu-bird-park-tour-6-hours/). Visitors can see birds of the region in a managed setting. Bird encounters in the park and sightings of free-ranging wild birds are different experiences and should not be confused in the tour's promises.

The following day, travellers visit the Argentine side of Iguazú and Devil's Throat. This is another nature experience, but geographically it belongs to [Argentina](/argentina/), which is visited on the full itinerary in addition to Brazil and Paraguay.

## How the conditions in the Chaco and Iguazú differ

The dry Chaco calls for protection against sun, dust and heat, along with drinking water. Near Iguazú, humidity, protection for belongings from spray, comfortable shoes for wet walkways and possible rain are more relevant. A single outfit for both nature stages will seldom be ideal.

Wildlife watching must account for distance and the behaviour of wild species. Fortín Toledo introduces conservation work; Laguna Capitán gives an opportunity to watch birds; and Brazil's Bird Park offers another, managed form of close observation. None of these turns the entire itinerary into a safari with guaranteed sightings.

The geography matters too: cultural and urban days in Paraguay separate the two nature regions. The published schedule does not include a direct “Chaco reserve to Iguazú Falls” transfer within one excursion day.

For more time devoted to wildlife, compare [nature tours featuring Brazil](/interests/wildlife/tours/brazil/), [Paraguay nature experiences](/interests/wildlife/tours/paraguay/) and [all multi-country nature and wildlife tours](/multi-country/interests/wildlife/). The complete list of trips including both countries is in the [Brazil + Paraguay catalogue](/multi-country/brazil_paraguay/).

## Frequently asked questions about wildlife in Brazil and Paraguay

### Can I see the rare tagua peccary?

The itinerary includes a visit to Fortín Toledo, where conservation work for this species takes place. Whether a particular animal can be seen depends on visitor access arrangements and local conditions; no sighting is guaranteed.

### Is flamingo watching included?

The tour includes a visit to Laguna Capitán, where flamingos and other birds may be found. Their presence close to the shore at the time of the visit cannot be predicted.

### Is this a safari through two countries?

No. The programme combines nature sites, history, museums and cities, while Brazil is represented mainly by Iguazú. The tour does not describe a continuous specialist two-country safari.

### Can I visit both sides of Iguazú Falls?

Yes. A panoramic day is scheduled on the Brazilian side, followed by a visit to the Argentine side and Devil's Throat the next day. Visiting the second side involves another border crossing.

lead: >-
  Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay come together on a route from Uruguay's Atlantic coast and wineries through Asunción and the dry Chaco to Iguazú Falls. On our 16-day tour, the Brazilian section begins at the border near Foz do Iguaçu, while the excursion to the Argentine side of the falls is an additional country visit. Before departure, internal flights, border formalities, season and payment methods in different currencies need to be agreed.
---

## Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay: how the route works

**Three very different South American experiences meet here:** Uruguayan cities beside the Río de la Plata and Atlantic, inland Paraguay and Brazil's tropical waterfalls. The contrasts extend beyond the scenery. A flight is required between [Uruguay](/uruguay/) and [Paraguay](/paraguay/), while the final stage in [Brazil](/brazil/) centres on the Iguazú border region.

Our selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with these as main countries. The published [16-day tour through Uruguay, Paraguay and Brazil](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/) travels from Montevideo through Asunción and the Chaco to Foz do Iguaçu. Its distinctive feature is the substantial Paraguayan section far beyond the capital, rather than a brief stop between airports.

| Stage | Main experiences |
|---|---|
| Uruguay | Montevideo, wineries, Punta del Este |
| Paraguay | Asunción, the Chaco, Laguna Capitán |
| Brazil | Iguazú Falls and Bird Park |

One excursion also crosses the border into Argentina to see the other side of Iguazú. **Argentina is an additional visit, not a separate multi-day stage**. That affects documents and the number of border crossings, even though this selection lists only three main countries.

## Uruguay: the capital, colonial heritage and the Atlantic coast

The journey starts in [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/). The city stretches along the Río de la Plata: the Rambla waterfront, historic centre, Independence Square and early 20th-century architecture offer an introduction to the capital without long road transfers. On this tour, city sightseeing begins on arrival day.

Next is [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/). Its historic quarter is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Founded by the Portuguese, the town was later contested by Portugal and Spain. The narrow cobbled streets preserve buildings reflecting both architectural traditions.

From Colonia, the itinerary continues to [Canelones](/uruguay/place/canelones/), a region of vineyards and wineries. The tour includes a tasting and lunch, focusing on the Tannat grape for which Uruguayan winemakers are well known. This stop matters if you want to discover both urban history and local gastronomy on the same journey.

Several days are then devoted to [Punta del Este](/uruguay/place/punta-del-este/): Mansa and Brava beaches, marina walks and free time by the ocean. The programme includes a visit to Casapueblo and a return to Montevideo before the flight. **The beach section takes place in Uruguay**, so a similar beach holiday should not be expected in Paraguay's Chaco or at Iguazú Falls.

## Paraguay: capital city, Chaco and smaller towns

After flying from Montevideo, travellers arrive in [Asunción](/paraguay/place/asuncion/). The programme includes the Museo del Barro, López Palace, the National Pantheon of Heroes and the Independence House Museum. Spanish colonial influences, Guaraní language and local craft traditions are all apparent in the capital. This is a substantial city stage, not merely an overnight transit stop.

The most unusual section is [Paraguay's Chaco](/paraguay/place/chaco/). Here are dry forests, hot plains, scattered settlements and long road journeys. The itinerary reaches [Filadelfia](/paraguay/place/filadelfia/), introduces Mennonite community history and includes Fortín Toledo Reserve. The Chaco needs its own time: it cannot reasonably be visited on a quick half-day excursion from Asunción.

The next day features [Laguna Capitán](/paraguay/place/laguna-capitan/), where waterbirds and shorebirds may be seen. Encounters with flamingos and other species depend on water levels, season and animal behaviour, so sightings cannot be guaranteed. The programme also includes an introduction to local communities and a return towards the capital.

The journey then continues through Areguá and San Bernardino to Colonia Independencia in Guairá's mountain area. Ceramics, crafts, family farms and natural scenery offer a different impression of Paraguay after the capital's museums and the dry Chaco. For other options, see [Paraguay tours](/paraguay/tour/) and the [country guide](/paraguay/).

## Brazil: both sides of Iguazú and the real border

The final part of the route involves a flight within Paraguay to Ciudad del Este, followed by a land transfer to [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). This is the Brazilian base for the falls. The next day, travellers visit the Brazilian viewing platforms, with broad panoramas over the cascades. The programme also lists Macuco Safari and the Bird Park; the terms of individual visits and availability of specific routes depend on operators and park arrangements.

One day is devoted to crossing to the Argentine side, near [Puerto Iguazú](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/). There, visitor walkways approach the water more closely, with Devil's Throat as the principal attraction. The visit requires actual entry to Argentina and subsequent departure or onward travel as determined by the confirmed tickets. **Entry to Argentina must not be assumed to be permitted simply because you are already in Brazil.**

Access to individual viewpoints, boat outings and trails depends on water levels, weather and current park rules. In October 2026, the Iguazú area had already experienced closures because of flooding, so the planned excursion needs an updated check closer to the visit. National park admission, boat travel and the Argentine-side visit are different components; the paid package must be read in the tour's specific terms.

## Flights, transfers and time at borders

The transport plan combines several types of movement. Uruguay features shorter city trips and road journeys between Montevideo, Colonia, Canelones and Punta del Este. Then comes **the Montevideo–Asunción flight**. In Paraguay, the itinerary makes a substantial overland circuit into the Chaco and back, followed by a flight to Ciudad del Este.

From Ciudad del Este, the group travels to Foz do Iguaçu, crossing the Paraguay–Brazil border. The Argentine-side excursion adds another border crossing and potentially a return entry, depending on final logistics. Total travel time includes transport waits, document checks and the journey itself. Planning such a day solely by the number of kilometres between two points is unrealistic.

When booking international flights home, confirm the final departure airport and do not assume the journey will end in the same city where it began in South America. The current itinerary finishes with an airport transfer after the Iguazú excursions; the specific connection needs to be arranged separately.

## Documents for three countries and the Argentine excursion

**Uruguay, Paraguay and Brazil assess entry permission separately.** Paraguay's migration authority requires foreign arrivals and departures to be registered through official border controls; travellers need valid travel documents, and some nationalities require a visa. Certain MERCOSUR citizens may travel on accepted national identity documents, but that benefit does not automatically apply to other nationalities.

Uruguay's visa requirements also depend on the passport. Where a visa is needed, consular rules establish a separate process and require confirmation of itinerary and financial circumstances. Brazil's entry conditions depend on nationality and purpose of travel. Finally, **the day on the Argentine side of Iguazú** requires the fourth country to be checked, even when the tour is marketed as a combination of three principal destinations.

Before paying for international flights, confirm all participants' passports, document validity, entry and re-entry conditions, requirements for minors, onward departure route and any transit countries. Clarify separately whether confirmed accommodation reservations and medical insurance are required. Visa rules are determined by the relevant national authorities, not by the fact that these destinations all lie in South America.

## Climate: what to wear for the coast, Chaco and waterfalls

Consider seasonal differences when choosing dates. **Uruguay** has a relatively temperate Southern Hemisphere climate compared with the tropics. December to February is the busy summer beach season in Punta del Este, although even in summer the coast can be windy. In cooler months, the journey retains its urban and gastronomic appeal, but beach holidays are a very different experience.

**Paraguay's Chaco** is substantially drier and can be hotter in clear weather, with long road journeys adding fatigue. The **Iguazú region** is more humid, with possible heavy rain and changes in river levels. Lightweight clothes, comfortable closed shoes, sun protection, a hat, raincoat and an extra layer for a cool coastal breeze work well together on this itinerary.

Check forecasts for the actual dates in Montevideo, Asunción, the Chaco and Foz do Iguaçu. A single “South America weather” forecast or average temperature across three countries is of little use for this journey.

## Money, currencies and costs

This route uses **Uruguayan pesos (UYU), Paraguayan guaraní (PYG) and Brazilian reais (BRL)**. Entry into Argentina may also call for Argentine pesos (ARS). US dollars are often a useful reserve, but will not replace local money for every small purchase. Exchange-office rates, ATM fees and card conversion can lead to noticeable differences in costs.

Visa and Mastercard cards issued by Russian banks do not work abroad, so travellers relying on such cards need an alternative payment method confirmed in advance. Account for possible conversion and cash withdrawal fees, not merely quoted exchange rates.

When comparing programme prices, distinguish international flights, the domestic flight between capitals, transport within Paraguay, hotels, meals, national park tickets and separate activities. A tour's name or appearance among VIP selections does not guarantee a particular hotel category or identical inclusions across all excursions. Confirm the actual contents of the selected offer: the terms of our [16-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/) are more important than general assumptions about regional travel.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many days do Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay require?

The current selection contains a 16-day programme: the opening days focus on Uruguay, followed by a substantial Paraguayan section and a finale around Iguazú. A shorter trip would require reducing the Chaco, beach time or the number of cities.

### Is Argentina included in the three-country tour?

The published itinerary includes the Argentine side of Iguazú Falls. Argentina is listed as an additional country because the main extended route runs through Uruguay, Paraguay and Brazil. Its entry conditions still need checking.

### Can the Chaco and Iguazú be combined without extra transfers?

They occupy different sections of the route. The Chaco requires an overland journey from Asunción and back, then a flight to Ciudad del Este and a crossing into Brazil. Both experiences cannot be combined into a single day.

### When is the best time for beaches in Uruguay?

The local summer, especially December to February, is generally more suitable for Punta del Este's beaches. But the Chaco's heat and rainfall around Iguazú must also be considered for the full trip; the best dates depend on which sections matter most.

### Are Macuco Safari and both sides of the waterfalls a single visit?

No. They are different activities with their own rules, admission procedures and possible water-level restrictions. Brazilian and Argentine viewing routes also involve separate border formalities. Check the paid excursion package for the specific itinerary.
